# Diagnostics

<!-- Generated by skill/plutonium/tools/gendiag from compiler/internal/diag. Do not edit; regenerate. -->

Every compile error ends with a code. `pluto explain E3301` prints the long explanation with an example; `pluto explain`
alone lists every code. Each row below gives the code, its name, what is wrong in one sentence and the usual fix.
Messages name the variables and lines involved; read them before this table. `--brief` (or `PLUTO_BRIEF=1`)
prints only the one-line message, without the code. Pick the first error in the output: later ones are often consequences.

How to read a diagnostic: `file:line:col: message`, then an indented explanation, a suggested fix, the specification
section (`section 18.3`: read `docs/spec/language/18-ownership-and-memory.md`) and the `pluto explain` line.

## E0001 to E0999: Go's type rules

These are the type checker's errors as Go has them (numbered as go/types numbers them), with the same meaning.

| Code | Name | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| E0002 | BlankPkgName | This error occurs when a package name is the blank identifier "_". | `pluto explain E0002` |
| E0004 | InvalidPkgUse | This error occurs when a package identifier is used outside of a selector expression. | `pluto explain E0004` |
| E0005 | BadImportPath | This error occurs when an import path is not valid. | `pluto explain E0005` |
| E0008 | UnusedImport | The file imports a package but never uses it. Plutonium, like Go, treats an unused import as an error, so that a file's imports always show what it really depends on. | Delete the import, or use the package. |
| E0009 | InvalidInitCycle | Package-level variables are initialized in an order where each comes after the ones its initial value uses. | `pluto explain E0009` |
| E0010 | DuplicateDecl | The same name is declared twice in one scope. Each name in a block, or at package level across all the package's files, must be declared once. | Rename one of them, or remove the duplicate. |
| E0011 | InvalidDeclCycle | A type, constant or variable is defined in terms of itself, so it has no well-defined size or value. | `pluto explain E0011` |
| E0013 | InvalidConstInit | A constant's value must be known when compiling: a literal, another constant, or an expression of those. | `pluto explain E0013` |
| E0014 | InvalidConstVal | This error occurs when a const value cannot be converted to its target type. | `pluto explain E0014` |
| E0015 | InvalidConstType | This error occurs when the underlying type in a const declaration is not a valid constant type. | `pluto explain E0015` |
| E0016 | UntypedNilUse | nil has no type of its own: it is the zero value of pointers, slices, interfaces and func values. A variable declared with := or var and no type takes the type of its value, and nil gives it none. | `pluto explain E0016` |
| E0017 | WrongAssignCount | The number of values on the right does not match the number of variables on the left. A call that returns several results must be assigned to that many variables; use _ for results you do not need. | `pluto explain E0017` |
| E0018 | UnassignableOperand | The left side of an assignment must be something that can hold a value: a variable, a pointer dereference, a field of an addressable struct, or a slice or array element. | `pluto explain E0018` |
| E0019 | NoNewVar | x := v declares new variables. Every name on the left already exists in this scope, so nothing would be declared. | `pluto explain E0019` |
| E0020 | MultiValAssignOp | This error occurs when an assignment operation (+=, *=, etc) does not have single-valued left-hand or right-hand side. | `pluto explain E0020` |
| E0021 | InvalidIfaceAssign | A value can be used as an interface only if its type has every method the interface lists, with the same parameters and results. | `pluto explain E0021` |
| E0022 | InvalidChanAssign | This error occurs when a chan assignment is invalid. | `pluto explain E0022` |
| E0023 | IncompatibleAssign | A value of one type is used where a different type is needed: in an assignment, a variable declaration, an argument or a return. | Convert explicitly with T(x) between number types, or use a function such as strconv.Atoi to turn text into a number. |
| E0024 | UnaddressableFieldAssign | This error occurs when trying to assign to a struct field in a map value. | `pluto explain E0024` |
| E0025 | NotAType | A name used as a type is not a type: it is a variable, constant, function or package. Check the spelling, and whether a local variable hides a type of the same name. | `pluto explain E0025` |
| E0026 | InvalidArrayLen | The length of an array type must be a constant integer that is not negative, since an array's size is fixed when compiling. | `pluto explain E0026` |
| E0027 | BlankIfaceMethod | This error occurs when a method name is '_'. | `pluto explain E0027` |
| E0028 | IncomparableMapKey | This error occurs when a map key type does not support the == and != operators. | `pluto explain E0028` |
| E0030 | InvalidPtrEmbed | This error occurs when an embedded field is of the pointer form *T, and T itself is itself a pointer, an unsafe.Pointer, or an interface. | `pluto explain E0030` |
| E0031 | BadRecv | This error occurs when a method declaration does not have exactly one receiver parameter. | `pluto explain E0031` |
| E0032 | InvalidRecv | This error occurs when a receiver type expression is not of the form T or *T, or T is a pointer type. | `pluto explain E0032` |
| E0033 | DuplicateFieldAndMethod | This error occurs when an identifier appears as both a field and method name. | `pluto explain E0033` |
| E0034 | DuplicateMethod | A type has two methods with the same name. Method names must be unique for each type, whatever their parameters; there is no overloading. | `pluto explain E0034` |
| E0035 | InvalidBlank | The blank identifier _ can be assigned to, to discard a value, but cannot be read. It is not a variable. | `pluto explain E0035` |
| E0036 | InvalidIota | This error occurs when the predeclared identifier iota is used outside of a constant declaration. | `pluto explain E0036` |
| E0037 | MissingInitBody | This error occurs when an init function is missing its body. | `pluto explain E0037` |
| E0039 | InvalidInitDecl | This error occurs when init is declared as anything other than a function. | `pluto explain E0039` |
| E0040 | InvalidMainDecl | In package main, the name main must be the function where the program starts. It cannot be a variable or type, and it cannot have type parameters. | `pluto explain E0040` |
| E0041 | TooManyValues | A function that returns several results is used where one value is expected. Assign the results to variables first, and use the one you need. | `pluto explain E0041` |
| E0042 | NotAnExpr | Something that is not a value, such as a type or a package name, is used where a value is needed. | `pluto explain E0042` |
| E0043 | TruncatedFloat | A constant with a fraction is used as an integer. Converting it would lose the fraction, which Plutonium, like Go, does not do silently for constants. | `pluto explain E0043` |
| E0044 | NumericOverflow | A constant does not fit in the type it is used as. Each integer type holds a fixed range: uint8 holds 0 to 255, int8 holds -128 to 127, and so on. | `pluto explain E0044` |
| E0045 | UndefinedOp | The operator is not defined for this type. For example, + works on numbers and constant strings, < works on numbers and strings, and ! works only on bools. | `pluto explain E0045` |
| E0046 | MismatchedTypes | The two operands of a binary operator, such as + or ==, must have the same type. Plutonium, like Go, never converts one to match the other, even between int and int64. | Convert one operand to the other's type with T(x). |
| E0047 | DivByZero | A constant division by zero. Dividing by a constant 0 is always wrong, so the compiler reports it rather than let it panic at run time. | `pluto explain E0047` |
| E0048 | NonNumericIncDec | ++ and -- work only on numbers. | `pluto explain E0048` |
| E0049 | UnaddressableOperand | & takes the address of a variable, a field of an addressable struct, a slice element or a composite literal. | `pluto explain E0049` |
| E0050 | InvalidIndirection | * follows a pointer to the value it points at. The operand here is not a pointer. | `pluto explain E0050` |
| E0051 | NonIndexableOperand | Only arrays, slices, strings, pointers to arrays, and generic types whose type set allows it can be indexed with [i]. | `pluto explain E0051` |
| E0052 | InvalidIndex | An index must be an integer that is not negative, and a constant index must be inside the bounds of an array or constant string. | `pluto explain E0052` |
| E0053 | SwappedSliceIndices | This error occurs when constant indices in a slice expression are decreasing in value. | `pluto explain E0053` |
| E0054 | NonSliceableOperand | This error occurs when a slice operation is applied to a value whose type is not sliceable, or is unaddressable. | `pluto explain E0054` |
| E0056 | InvalidShiftCount | The count of a shift, the right operand of << or >>, must be an integer that is not negative. | `pluto explain E0056` |
| E0057 | InvalidShiftOperand | This error occurs when the shifted operand is not an integer. | `pluto explain E0057` |
| E0058 | InvalidReceive | This error occurs when there is a channel receive from a value that is either not a channel, or is a send-only channel. | `pluto explain E0058` |
| E0059 | InvalidSend | This error occurs when there is a channel send to a value that is not a channel, or is a receive-only channel. | `pluto explain E0059` |
| E0060 | DuplicateLitKey | A composite literal gives the same index or key twice. | `pluto explain E0060` |
| E0061 | MissingLitKey | This error occurs when a map literal is missing a key expression. | `pluto explain E0061` |
| E0062 | InvalidLitIndex | This error occurs when the key in a key-value element of a slice or array literal is not an integer constant. | `pluto explain E0062` |
| E0063 | OversizeArrayLit | This error occurs when an array literal exceeds its length. | `pluto explain E0063` |
| E0064 | MixedStructLit | A struct literal either names every field it sets (Point{X: 1, Y: 2}) or lists a value for every field in order (Point{1, 2}). | `pluto explain E0064` |
| E0065 | InvalidStructLit | This error occurs when a positional struct literal has an incorrect number of values. | `pluto explain E0065` |
| E0066 | MissingLitField | The struct literal names a field that the struct type does not have. Check the spelling; field names are case-sensitive. | `pluto explain E0066` |
| E0067 | DuplicateLitField | The struct literal sets the same field twice. | `pluto explain E0067` |
| E0068 | UnexportedLitField | The literal sets a field of another package's struct whose name starts with a lower-case letter. Such fields are private to their package. | `pluto explain E0068` |
| E0069 | InvalidLitField | This error occurs when a field name is not a valid identifier. | `pluto explain E0069` |
| E0070 | UntypedLit | This error occurs when a composite literal omits a required type identifier. | `pluto explain E0070` |
| E0071 | InvalidLit | This error occurs when a composite literal expression does not match its type. | `pluto explain E0071` |
| E0072 | AmbiguousSelector | This error occurs when a selector is ambiguous. | `pluto explain E0072` |
| E0073 | UndeclaredImportedName | The package has no exported name like this. Only names that start with an upper-case letter can be used from other packages. | `pluto explain E0073` |
| E0074 | UnexportedName | The name starts with a lower-case letter, so it is private to the package that declares it and cannot be used from another package. | `pluto explain E0074` |
| E0075 | UndeclaredName | The name is not declared in any scope that reaches this point. It may be misspelled (names are case-sensitive), declared in a block that has ended, or belong to a package that is not imported. | `pluto explain E0075` |
| E0076 | MissingFieldOrMethod | The type has no field or method with this name. Check the spelling: names are case-sensitive, and another package's names must start with an upper-case letter. | `pluto explain E0076` |
| E0077 | BadDotDotDotSyntax | This error occurs when a "..." occurs in a context where it is not valid. | `pluto explain E0077` |
| E0078 | NonVariadicDotDotDot | This error occurs when a "..." is used on the final argument to a non-variadic function. | `pluto explain E0078` |
| E0081 | InvalidDotDotDot | This error occurs when a "..." is used in a non-variadic built-in function. | `pluto explain E0081` |
| E0082 | UncalledBuiltin | A builtin function such as len or cap is used as a value. Builtins can only be called; wrap the call in a function literal if you need a func value. | `pluto explain E0082` |
| E0084 | InvalidCap | cap takes an array or a pointer to one, a slice or a channel. Unlike len, it does not call methods: a library container or a ring reports its capacity with a method of its own. | Call the type's Cap method instead. |
| E0085 | InvalidClose | This error occurs when close(...) is called with an argument that is not of channel type, or that is a receive-only channel. | `pluto explain E0085` |
| E0086 | InvalidCopy | This error occurs when the arguments are not of slice type or do not have compatible type. | `pluto explain E0086` |
| E0088 | InvalidDelete | This error occurs when the delete built-in function is called with a first argument that is not a map. | `pluto explain E0088` |
| E0090 | InvalidLen | len takes a string, an array or a pointer to one, a slice, a map, a channel, an owned, shared or synced array, or a value whose type has a method Len() int, such as a library container or a ring; len(E) of an enum type E is... | Pass a value of one of these types, or store the value in a variable first. |
| E0091 | SwappedMakeArgs | This error occurs when make is called with three arguments, and its length argument is larger than its capacity argument. | `pluto explain E0091` |
| E0092 | InvalidMake | This error occurs when make is called with an unsupported type argument. | `pluto explain E0092` |
| E0094 | InvalidAssert | A type assertion x.(T) asks which concrete type an interface value holds, so x must be an interface. | `pluto explain E0094` |
| E0095 | ImpossibleAssert | The type in the assertion does not have every method of the interface, so no value of the interface can hold it, and the assertion would always fail. | `pluto explain E0095` |
| E0096 | InvalidConversion | This conversion is not allowed. T(x) converts between number types, between types with the same underlying type, and between pointers and unsafe.Pointer. | `pluto explain E0096` |
| E0097 | InvalidUntypedConversion | This error occurs when there is no valid implicit conversion from an untyped value satisfying the type constraints of the context in which it is used. | `pluto explain E0097` |
| E0098 | BadOffsetofSyntax | This error occurs when unsafe.Offsetof is called with an argument that is not a selector expression. | `pluto explain E0098` |
| E0099 | InvalidOffsetof | This error occurs when unsafe.Offsetof is called with a method selector, rather than a field selector, or when the field is embedded via a pointer. | `pluto explain E0099` |
| E0100 | UnusedExpr | The expression computes a value and throws it away, so it has no effect. A statement must do something: call a function, assign, send, and so on. | `pluto explain E0100` |
| E0101 | UnusedVar | A local variable is declared but its value is never used. Plutonium, like Go, treats this as an error, because it often means a mistake, such as assigning to the wrong variable. | Remove the variable, use it, or assign it to _ for now. |
| E0102 | MissingReturn | A function that declares results must end every path through its body with a return statement (or a panic, or an endless loop). | Add a return at the end, or a panic if that point can never be reached. |
| E0103 | WrongResultCount | The return statement gives a different number of values than the function declares as results. Return one value for each result, in order. | `pluto explain E0103` |
| E0104 | OutOfScopeResult | This error occurs when the name of a value implicitly returned by an empty return statement is shadowed in a nested scope. | `pluto explain E0104` |
| E0105 | InvalidCond | The condition of an if or for statement must be a bool. Plutonium, like Go, does not treat numbers or pointers as true or false; compare explicitly. | `pluto explain E0105` |
| E0106 | InvalidPostDecl | This error occurs when there is a declaration in a for-loop post statement. | `pluto explain E0106` |
| E0108 | InvalidIterVar | This error occurs when two iteration variables are used while ranging over a channel. | `pluto explain E0108` |
| E0109 | InvalidRangeExpr | for range works over arrays, slices, strings, integers, channels, enum types and iterator functions. | `pluto explain E0109` |
| E0110 | MisplacedBreak | break must be inside a for, switch or select statement. | `pluto explain E0110` |
| E0111 | MisplacedContinue | continue must be inside a for statement. | `pluto explain E0111` |
| E0112 | MisplacedFallthrough | This error occurs when a fallthrough statement is not within an expression switch. | `pluto explain E0112` |
| E0113 | DuplicateCase | A switch lists the same constant value in two cases. Only the first could ever match. | `pluto explain E0113` |
| E0114 | DuplicateDefault | This error occurs when a type or expression switch has multiple default clauses. | `pluto explain E0114` |
| E0115 | BadTypeKeyword | This error occurs when a .(type) expression is used anywhere other than a type switch. | `pluto explain E0115` |
| E0116 | InvalidTypeSwitch | This error occurs when .(type) is used on an expression that is not of interface type. | `pluto explain E0116` |
| E0117 | InvalidExprSwitch | A case value cannot be compared with the switch value: their types differ, or the type cannot be compared with ==. | `pluto explain E0117` |
| E0118 | InvalidSelectCase | This error occurs when a select case is not a channel send or receive. | `pluto explain E0118` |
| E0119 | UndeclaredLabel | This error occurs when an undeclared label is jumped to. | `pluto explain E0119` |
| E0120 | DuplicateLabel | This error occurs when a label is declared more than once. | `pluto explain E0120` |
| E0121 | MisplacedLabel | This error occurs when a break or continue label is not on a for, switch, or select statement. | `pluto explain E0121` |
| E0122 | UnusedLabel | A label is declared but no break, continue or goto uses it. Remove it. | `pluto explain E0122` |
| E0123 | JumpOverDecl | This error occurs when a label jumps over a variable declaration. | `pluto explain E0123` |
| E0124 | JumpIntoBlock | This error occurs when a forward jump goes to a label inside a nested block. | `pluto explain E0124` |
| E0125 | InvalidMethodExpr | This error occurs when a pointer method is called but the argument is not addressable. | `pluto explain E0125` |
| E0126 | WrongArgCount | The call passes a different number of arguments than the function has parameters. The message shows the arguments given (have) and the parameters (want). | `pluto explain E0126` |
| E0127 | InvalidCall | Only functions, methods and func values can be called. The expression before the parentheses is something else, or a type used in a way that is not a conversion. | `pluto explain E0127` |
| E0128 | UnusedResults | The result of this call must be used. Builtins such as len and cap, and conversions, have no effect other than their result. | `pluto explain E0128` |
| E0129 | InvalidDefer | This error occurs when a deferred expression is not a function call, for example if the expression is a type conversion. | `pluto explain E0129` |
| E0130 | InvalidGo | This error occurs when a go expression is not a function call, for example if the expression is a type conversion. | `pluto explain E0130` |
| E0131 | BadDecl | This error occurs when a declaration has invalid syntax. | `pluto explain E0131` |
| E0132 | RepeatedDecl | This error occurs when an identifier occurs more than once on the left hand side of a short variable declaration. | `pluto explain E0132` |
| E0133 | InvalidUnsafeAdd | This error occurs when unsafe.Add is called with a length argument that is not of integer type. It also occurs if it is used in a package compiled for a language version before go1.17. | `pluto explain E0133` |
| E0134 | InvalidUnsafeSlice | This error occurs when unsafe.Slice is called with a pointer argument that is not of pointer type or a length argument that is not of integer type, negative, or out of bounds. | `pluto explain E0134` |
| E0136 | NotAGenericType | Type arguments in square brackets are given to a type that has no type parameters. | `pluto explain E0136` |
| E0137 | WrongTypeArgCount | A generic function or type gets a different number of type arguments than it has type parameters. Give one for each, or leave out the trailing ones that can be inferred from the arguments. | `pluto explain E0137` |
| E0138 | CannotInferTypeArgs | A generic function was called without type arguments, and the compiler could not work them out from the call's arguments. | `pluto explain E0138` |
| E0139 | InvalidTypeArg | A type argument does not satisfy its type parameter's constraint. The constraint is an interface that lists the methods the type needs, or the set of types allowed (such as ~int \| ~float64). | `pluto explain E0139` |
| E0140 | InvalidInstanceCycle | This error occurs when an invalid cycle is detected within the instantiation graph. | `pluto explain E0140` |
| E0141 | InvalidUnion | This error occurs when an embedded union or approximation element is not valid. | `pluto explain E0141` |
| E0142 | MisplacedConstraintIface | This error occurs when a constraint-type interface is used outside of constraint position. | `pluto explain E0142` |
| E0144 | MisplacedTypeParam | This error occurs when a type parameter is used in a place where it is not permitted. | `pluto explain E0144` |
| E0145 | InvalidUnsafeSliceData | This error occurs when unsafe.SliceData is called with an argument that is not of slice type. It also occurs if it is used in a package compiled for a language version before go1.20. | `pluto explain E0145` |
| E0146 | InvalidUnsafeString | This error occurs when unsafe.String is called with a length argument that is not of integer type, negative, or out of bounds. | `pluto explain E0146` |
| E0148 | InvalidClear | This error occurs when clear is called with an argument that is not of map or slice type. | `pluto explain E0148` |
| E0149 | TypeTooLarge | This error occurs if unsafe.Sizeof or unsafe.Offsetof is called with an expression whose type is too large. | `pluto explain E0149` |
| E0150 | InvalidMinMaxOperand | This error occurs if min or max is called with an operand that cannot be ordered because it does not support the < operator. | `pluto explain E0150` |

## E1000 to E1999: syntax errors

The parser. The message names the token it did not expect.

| Code | Name | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| E1000 | SyntaxError | The parser could not read this part of the file as Plutonium. The message says what it expected and what it found instead. | `pluto explain E1000` |
| E1001 | UnexpectedToken | The parser expected one thing here and found another. The mistake is often just before the position shown: a missing comma, bracket or operator, or a keyword used as a name. | `pluto explain E1001` |
| E1002 | UnclosedBlock | The file ended while a block was still open: a { has no matching }. The parser reports the error at the end of the file, but the missing } belongs somewhere earlier. | `pluto explain E1002` |
| E1003 | StmtOutsideFunc | Outside a function, a file may contain only declarations: package, import, const, var, type and func. | Declare a package-level variable with var: `var count = 1` |
| E1004 | MissingSemicolon | Statements end at the end of a line, or at a semicolon. The parser found the end of one statement and then more text on the same line that does not start a new one. | `pluto explain E1004` |
| E1005 | MissingOperand | The parser expected a value here, such as a name, a number or a call, and found an operator or keyword instead. | `pluto explain E1005` |
| E1006 | BraceOnNextLine | The { that opens a block must be on the same line as the if, for, switch or func that it belongs to. | `pluto explain E1006` |
| E1007 | BadImportDecl | An import names a package with a string in double quotes, and all imports come right after the package clause, before any other declaration. | `pluto explain E1007` |
| E1008 | BadLiteral | A string, rune or number is not written correctly, or the file contains a character that is not allowed outside strings and comments. | `pluto explain E1008` |
| E1009 | MissingPackage | Every source file starts with a package clause, such as package main, before anything else except comments. | `pluto explain E1009` |
| E1011 | IfaceMethodTParams | Methods may have type parameters of their own, but an interface cannot declare such a method. A call through an interface does not know which type's method it reaches, so it could not pick an instance of a generic method. | `pluto explain E1011` |
| E1012 | GoStatement | A task is started with the task statement, written like a call: task worker(jobs). The word go is reserved so that a statement that starts with it gets this message, but it starts nothing in Plutonium. | To start a task, write task in place of go: `task worker(jobs)` |
| E1013 | OrOperand | An or clause tests the error that a call returns, so or must come right after a call: a function, method or function value with its arguments. | Make the call alone the operand of or, and use its values in a statement after it: `n := strconv.Atoi(s) or return` |

## E2000 to E2499: Plutonium rules checked by the type checker

Removed constructs, enums, unions, packed types, defaults, the or clause, `errors.New`, sendability, indexing containers.

| Code | Name | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| E2004 | RecoverNotPermitted | In Plutonium, panic stops the program. A hosted program first runs the pending deferred calls, as Go does, but control never returns to the function that panicked, so there is nothing for recover to catch. | Return an error instead: `func parse(s string) (int, error) {` |
| E2005 | ReflectNotPermitted | Plutonium has no reflect package. Reflection needs a description of every type in the running program. | Use a type switch, or generics, to handle values of several types. |
| E2006 | ComplexNotPermitted | Plutonium has no complex number types (complex64 and complex128) and no complex, real or imag builtins. | Use a struct: `type Complex struct{ Re, Im float64 }` |
| E2007 | MissingAllocatorType | new and make take an optional allocator as their last argument. Its type, Allocator, is declared in package pluto/rt, which this build could not find. | Check that PLUTOROOT, if set, points at a directory that contains pluto/rt. |
| E2008 | ErrorsNewNotConstant | errors.New takes only a constant message, such as a string literal. The compiler makes an error type for each place errors.New is called, with a counter in the program image, so the message must be known when compiling. | To include values in the message: `return fmt.Errorf("open %s: not found", name)` |
| E2009 | BadMainSignature | func main takes no arguments. It may return nothing, as in Go, or one int64, which becomes the program's exit status. | Either form works: `func main() { ... }` |
| E2010 | NotSendable | A value that crosses tasks, as the argument or receiver of a task statement or as the element of a channel, must be sendable. | Count the references atomically: `type Job struct {` |
| E2011 | FrameViewSent | This value points into the current function's stack frame: the address of a local variable or of part of one, a slice of a local array, or the address of a composite literal. | Start the work with a sync.Scope, which waits for it before its block ends: `var s sync.Scope` |
| E2012 | InvalidUTF8String | Every string in Plutonium holds valid UTF-8 text, so a string literal whose escapes spell out bytes that are not valid UTF-8 is an error. | Keep binary data in bytes: `magic := []byte{0x7f, 'E', 'L', 'F'}` |
| E2013 | AppendNotPermitted | Plutonium has no append. In Go, append grows a slice by allocating a larger array behind the program's back, and the garbage collector frees the old one. | To build a sequence that grows: `v := vec.New[int]()` |
| E2014 | MakeSliceNotPermitted | Plutonium has no make for slices. In Go, make([]T, n) allocates an array that the garbage collector frees when no slice refers to it. | Make a vec.Vec, which owns the array: `buf := vec.Make[byte](n)` |
| E2015 | BytesToStringNotPermitted | Plutonium has no string(b) for a byte slice b. Every string holds valid UTF-8 text, but a slice of bytes can hold anything. | To check the bytes and handle bad input: `s, err := strings.FromUTF8(b)` |
| E2016 | StringToSliceNotPermitted | Plutonium has no []byte(s) or []rune(s) for a string s. In Go the conversion allocates a new slice and the garbage collector frees it later. | To keep a copy that you own: `b := strings.Bytes(s)` |
| E2017 | IntToStringNotPermitted | string(i) of an integer does not give the digits of i. In Go it gives the character whose code is i, so string(65) is "A" and string(n) for n := 65 is "A" too, not "65". | To make the character with code i: `s := string(rune(i))` |
| E2018 | NotPortable | A type parameter declared [T portable] stands for a value that can be sent between address spaces, such as two operating system processes that share no memory. | Send the bytes in a fixed-size array, with their length as a number: `type Header struct {` |
| E2019 | StringSliceNotPermitted | A string cannot be cut with a slice expression such as s[i:j]. Every string holds valid UTF-8 text, and a character can take up to four bytes, so a cut at an arbitrary byte offset could split one in two. | To take the substring from i to j: `sub := strings.Slice(s, i, j)` |
| E2020 | UnsendableToError | Every error value may be sent to another task, so a value can become an error (or an interface that embeds error) only if its type is sendable. | Hold the data in a synced[T], which counts atomically: `type Failure struct {` |
| E2021 | BadPackedBytePlacement | A big-endian packed type with a byte array, a []byte or no backing numbers its bits byte by byte, and stores a field of several bytes with its most significant byte first. | Put the field in a packed type of its own with an integer backing, and use that type as a field. The nested type is then laid out as an integer, whatever the bytes around it. |
| E2022 | PerCPUAccess | A //pu:percpu variable has one copy for each processor. | Put the use inside a region where the task cannot move: `rt.DisablePreemption()` |
| E2023 | PerCPUPointer | &v for a //pu:percpu variable v points into the copy of the processor that runs the code that takes it. | Use the variable by name inside the region, or keep a copy of its value: `rt.DisablePreemption()` |
| E2101 | BadPackedBacking | The backing type of a packed type says how its bits are stored. It must be an unsigned or signed integer type (uint32), an array of bytes ([8]byte), or []byte. | `pluto explain E2101` |
| E2102 | PackedTooLarge | The fields of a packed type are laid out one after another, from bit 0. Their widths add up to more bits than the backing type holds. | Use a larger backing type, make fields narrower, or leave the backing type out so the size follows the fields. |
| E2103 | BadBitField | A bit field is written bits[T, N]: N bits read as type T. T must be an integer type at least N bits wide, an enum, or bool with N equal to 1. | `pluto explain E2103` |
| E2104 | BadPackedField | A field of a packed type must have a fixed bit layout: an integer, bool, float, packed type, or an array of those. | `pluto explain E2104` |
| E2105 | BadPackedLiteral | A packed literal must name each field it sets, as field: value. The fields of a packed type have no order a literal could follow, since reserved bits sit between them. | `pluto explain E2105` |
| E2106 | WrongWrapperArgs | volatile takes one type argument: volatile[T]. aligned and ring take a type and a constant: aligned[T, N] and ring[T, N]. | `pluto explain E2106` |
| E2107 | NotPowerOfTwo | The alignment of aligned[T, N] and the size of ring[T, N] must be a power of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. | `pluto explain E2107` |
| E2108 | BadVolatileElem | volatile[T] makes every read and write of T exactly one load or store. That is only possible for a value the processor moves in one instruction: an integer, a bool, a pointer, or a packed type backed by an integer. | `pluto explain E2108` |
| E2109 | BadWrapperSize | The second argument of aligned[T, N] and ring[T, N] must be a positive integer constant, since the layout is fixed when compiling. | `pluto explain E2109` |
| E2110 | RingLiteralNotEmpty | A ring literal cannot list elements. Write an empty literal, or use the zero value, and add elements with Push. | `pluto explain E2110` |
| E2111 | BigEndianPackedArray | A big-endian packed type cannot have an array field whose elements are wider than one byte, whatever its backing. | Declare one field for each element instead, or use an array of bytes and put the values together yourself. |
| E2201 | MisplacedDefault | Default parameter values are allowed only on the parameters of a declared function or method. | `pluto explain E2201` |
| E2202 | VariadicDefault | A variadic function (one whose last parameter is ...T) cannot have default values. | `pluto explain E2202` |
| E2203 | MissingDefault | A call may leave out only trailing parameters. So once a parameter has a default value, every parameter after it needs one too. | `pluto explain E2203` |
| E2204 | SharedDefault | A parameter with a default value needs a name and type of its own. In a, b int = 1 it is unclear whether the default belongs to a, to b, or to both. | `pluto explain E2204` |
| E2205 | DefaultRefersToParam | A default value is evaluated by the caller, in the scope where the function is declared, before the function runs. | `pluto explain E2205` |
| E2301 | MisplacedEnum | An enum type can only be the type of a type definition, type E enum { ... }. It cannot be written inline in a variable or field, or be an alias, because its members are reached through its name (E.Member). | `pluto explain E2301` |
| E2302 | GenericEnum | An enum type cannot have type parameters. Its members are constants of one fixed integer type. | `pluto explain E2302` |
| E2303 | BadEnumBase | The type after the enum keyword is the integer type that holds the enum's values. It must be an integer type such as uint8 or int32. | `pluto explain E2303` |
| E2304 | EmptyEnum | An enum needs at least one member, and one member must have the value 0, since that is the zero value of the type. | `pluto explain E2304` |
| E2305 | BlankEnumMember | Every member of an enum needs a name. To skip a value, give the next member an explicit value instead. | `pluto explain E2305` |
| E2306 | DuplicateEnumValue | Two members of an enum have the same value. Each value must belong to one member, so that converting a number to the enum, and printing a value's name, give one answer. | `pluto explain E2306` |
| E2307 | EnumWithoutZero | A variable of an enum type starts as 0, like every Plutonium variable. So one member must have the value 0, or a fresh variable would hold a value that is not a member. | Add a member for the zero value, often named None, Unknown or Invalid. |
| E2308 | EnumOverflow | A member's value does not fit in the enum's integer type. Pick a wider type after the enum keyword, or leave the type out so the compiler picks one that fits. | `pluto explain E2308` |
| E2309 | BadEnumValue | The value of an enum member must be a constant integer expression, such as 5, 1 << 3 or another constant, since members are constants fixed when compiling. | `pluto explain E2309` |
| E2310 | EnumSelfReference | An enum's member values cannot use the enum being declared, because those values are what decides the enum's integer type. | `pluto explain E2310` |
| E2311 | UnexportedEnumMember | Enum members follow Go's rule for names: a member whose name starts with a lower-case letter is visible only inside its own package. | `pluto explain E2311` |
| E2312 | MissingEnumCase | A switch on an enum value that has no default case must list every member. That way, adding a member to the enum shows every switch that needs to handle it. | Add a case for each missing member, or a default case if the remaining members share one action. |
| E2313 | BadEnumConversion | Only integers convert to an enum, and a constant converts only if it is the value of a member. Anything else would make an enum value that is not a member. | `pluto explain E2313` |
| E2314 | UncheckedEnumConversion | A number that is not a constant may not be the value of any member, so converting it to an enum needs a check. | Use the comma-ok form: `c, ok := Color(n)` |
| E2315 | UntypedEnumConstant | A number written in the source is not a member of an enum, so it cannot be used where an enum value is expected. | Name the member: `var c Color = Color.Green` |
| E2316 | EnumArithmetic | Enum values can be compared, but not added, multiplied, shifted or combined with bitwise operators, since the result would usually not be a member. | Convert to an integer first: `next := int(c) + 1` |
| E2317 | RangeOverEnumValue | To loop over the members of an enum, range over the enum type itself, not over a value of it. | Range over the type: `for c := range Color {` |
| E2318 | NotEnumType | This operation needs an enum type, such as len(E) or for v := range E, and the type given is not an enum. | `pluto explain E2318` |
| E2401 | MisplacedUnion | A union type can only be the type of a type definition, type U union { ... }. It cannot be written inline in a variable or field, or be an alias, because its variants are reached through its name (U.V). | `pluto explain E2401` |
| E2402 | GenericPackedUnion | A packed union cannot have type parameters. Its layout is fixed bit by bit by its backing type, its tag and its fields, so it cannot depend on a type argument. | `pluto explain E2402` |
| E2403 | EmptyUnion | A union value holds one of its variants, so a union needs at least one. Variants are written like struct fields: a name, and a payload type if the variant carries data. | `pluto explain E2403` |
| E2404 | BadVariantDecl | Each variant of a union has a name of its own, which is not _, followed by its payload type if it has one. | `pluto explain E2404` |
| E2405 | TooManyVariants | A union numbers its variants with a tag of at most 16 bits, so it can have at most 65536 variants. Group related variants into a variant whose payload is another union or an enum. | `pluto explain E2405` |
| E2406 | UnionOwnerPayload | This payload is an owner: an owned[T] box, or a type declared owner, such as a file or a vec.Vec. A union that holds one owns the payload of the variant it holds. | Declare the union as an owner: `type Slot owner union {` |
| E2407 | BadUnionTag | A packed union has a backing type, which fixes its size, and exactly one named field before its variants: the tag. | `pluto explain E2407` |
| E2408 | BadVariantCase | The values after case in a packed union variant are the tag values that select it. | `pluto explain E2408` |
| E2409 | VariantNotType | A variant of a union is not a type. U.V(x) and U.V{...} make a value of the union type U holding the variant, and a type switch on a union gives you the payload of the variant it holds, which has the payload's own type. | `pluto explain E2409` |
| E2410 | UnknownVariant | The union has no variant with this name, or the type before the dot is not a union, so it has no variants at all. | `pluto explain E2410` |
| E2411 | UnexportedVariant | Union variants follow Go's rule for names: a variant whose name starts with a lower-case letter is visible only inside its own package. | `pluto explain E2411` |
| E2412 | UnionLiteral | A union value holds one of its variants, so a literal must name the variant: U.V{...} for a variant whose payload is a struct, array or packed type, or U.V(payload) for any variant with a payload. | `pluto explain E2412` |
| E2413 | NotAVariant | A type switch on a union value, and a type assertion on one, name the union's own variants: U.V, or in a case of the switch the bare name V. | `pluto explain E2413` |
| E2414 | MissingVariantCase | A type switch on a union value that has no default case must name every variant. That way, adding a variant to the union shows every switch that needs to handle it. | Add a case for each missing variant, or a default case if the remaining variants share one action. A switch that names every variant needs no default to end a function. |
| E2415 | PackedUnionNoDefault | A packed union's bits usually come from hardware or from converting a raw value, so its tag may hold any value its bits allow, including values no variant names. | Add a default case that handles the other values. |
| E2451 | MissingIndexMethod | Library containers such as vec.Vec and hash.Map are indexed through methods. x[k] calls x.Index(k), x[k] = v calls x.SetIndex(k, v), and v, ok := x[k] calls x.IndexOk(k). | To support v, ok := x[k], add: `func (m *Table) IndexOk(k string) (int, bool) {` |
| E2452 | BadIndexMethod | The indexing methods have fixed forms, so that x[k] can be turned into a call: Index(k K) V, SetIndex(k K, v V) and IndexOk(k K) (V, bool). | `pluto explain E2452` |
| E2453 | IndexMethodMismatch | The indexing methods of one type must agree: Index, SetIndex and IndexOk take the same key type K, and use the same element type V. | `pluto explain E2453` |
| E2454 | ContainerIndexAddress | x[k] on a container calls its Index method, which returns a copy of the element. | Ask for the pointer by name: `p := v.Ptr(i)` |
| E2455 | ContainerElemAssign | x[k] on a container is a copy that its Index method returns, so assigning to a field or element of it would change only the copy. | Store the changed element back: `p := v[i]` |
| E2456 | RangeOverContainer | A for range loop over a value that is not a string, integer, array, slice, map, channel or function calls the value's All method and ranges over the iterator it returns, an iter.Seq or iter.Seq2. | Add an All method: `func (t *T) All() iter.Seq2[string, int] {` |
| E2457 | UnaddressableContainer | The container's indexing method has a pointer receiver, so x[k] needs the address of x. Here x is a value that has no address, such as the result of a function call. | Store it in a variable first: `m := load()` |
| E2458 | BadRangeMethod | A for range loop over a container calls its All method, which must take no arguments and return an iterator: a function of the form func(yield func(K, V) bool), such as iter.Seq[V] or iter.Seq2[K, V]. | `pluto explain E2458` |
| E2459 | UnaddressableRange | A for range loop over a container calls its All method. That method has a pointer receiver, so the loop needs the address of the container. | Store it in a variable first: `m := load()` |
| E2461 | OrNotFunctionCall | An or clause tests the error that a function returns as its last result. | Remove the or clause, or call a function that returns an error. |
| E2462 | OrNoError | The call before or must return a result of type error last, and the type must be error itself. A function that returns no error, or no result at all, cannot fail in a way that or can see. | Return the error as an error: `func parse(s string) (int, error)` |
| E2463 | OrClauseCompletes | The clause of an or statement runs when the call failed, and the code after the statement uses the values the call did not produce. | End the clause with a statement that leaves: `cfg := load(path) or {` |
| E2464 | OrNoErrorResult | An unbraced return with no operands in an or clause returns err as the function's last result. This function has no result of type error last, so there is nowhere to put err, and returning without it would drop the error. | Handle the error in a block clause: `load(path) or {` |
| E2465 | OrPostStmt | The post statement of a for statement runs at the end of each iteration. An or statement cannot be the post statement, since a break or continue in its clause would end or repeat the iteration that is ending. | Test the error in the body: `for i := 0; i < n; {` |

## E2500 to E2999: Plutonium rules checked while compiling

Directives, C and assembly linkage, per-CPU variables, kernel rules, `defer`, `task`, schedulers, interrupt context.

| Code | Name | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| E2500 | NotYetSupported | The program is valid, but this compiler cannot compile this construct yet. It stops with an error rather than produce wrong code. | `pluto explain E2500` |
| E2510 | ExternWithBody | //pu:extern says that the function is written in C or assembly and linked in under the given symbol. | `pluto explain E2510` |
| E2511 | BadCSignature | Functions marked //pu:extern or //pu:export are called with the C calling convention. Their parameters and results must be types C has: integers, floats, bools, pointers, and structs and arrays of those. | Pass a pointer and a length: `func write(fd int32, buf *byte, n uint64) int64` |
| E2512 | DuplicateExport | Two functions are exported under the same symbol name with //pu:export, or the name is already used by another symbol. | `pluto explain E2512` |
| E2513 | GenericExport | A generic function is compiled once for each set of type arguments it is used with, so there is no single function to export under one C symbol. | Export a wrapper |
| E2520 | KernelFloat | In kernel mode, functions may not use floating point. | Mark the function, and save the state around calls: `func scale(x float64) float64 { return x * 1.5 }` |
| E2521 | UnprintableArgument | print and println can write a boolean, an integer (an enum too), a floating-point number, a string, or a type whose underlying type is one of these. | Convert an integer field, or use fmt: `println(int32(fd))` |
| E2530 | DeferInLoop | A defer statement in a loop would add a deferred call on every iteration, and each needs room in the function's stack frame until it returns. | Move the body into a function: `for _, name := range names {` |
| E2531 | TooManyDefers | A function may contain at most 64 defer statements. Each has a fixed slot in the stack frame. Split the function into smaller ones. | `pluto explain E2531` |
| E2532 | DeferBuiltin | This builtin cannot be deferred directly. Wrap the call in a function literal and defer that. | Defer a function literal: `defer func() { n = len(s) }()` |
| E2534 | DeferLitCapture | A function literal deferred in the body of a loop over a function runs when the enclosing function returns, after the loop body has returned. | Pass the loop variable as an argument: `for x := range seq {` |
| E2542 | ErrorsNewValue | errors.New must be called directly. Each place that calls it gets its own error type, made when compiling, so taking errors.New as a value, or deferring it, has no call site to make that type for. | `pluto explain E2542` |
| E2550 | PerCPUInit | A per-CPU variable can only be initialized with a constant. Package initialization runs before any processor has its per-CPU block, so there is nowhere to store a value computed at run time. | `pluto explain E2550` |
| E2551 | PerCPUMode | //pu:percpu variables are reached through the GS segment register, which only a kernel sets up. Build with --mode kernel, or remove the directive. | `pluto explain E2551` |
| E2552 | PerCPUSection | A per-CPU variable always lives in the .percpu section, so it cannot also be placed in another section with //pu:section. | `pluto explain E2552` |
| E2560 | StackDirective | //pu:stack sets the size of the stack a hosted program runs on: the runtime reserves that much address space before main starts. | Remove the directive and set up the stack in the program's start code |
| E2561 | StackSize | //pu:stack takes a size in bytes, with an optional K, M or G suffix, from 64K to 64G. | Use a size in range: `func main() { ... }` |
| E2570 | InterruptDecl | A //pu:interrupt function is entered by the processor, not called by Plutonium code. | `pluto explain E2570` |
| E2571 | InterruptSig | An interrupt handler receives what the processor pushes on the stack: a pointer to the interrupt frame, and for some exceptions an error code. | Use one of these signatures: `func timer(frame *x86.InterruptFrame)` |
| E2572 | GateArg | x86.InterruptGate and x86.TrapGate build the entry of the interrupt table that enters a handler, and the compiler puts the handler's address in it. | Pass the name of a handler of the form the constructor takes: `func timer(f *x86.InterruptFrame) { ... }` |
| E2573 | InterruptHandlerV | An interrupt handler saves every register and returns with iretq, so ordinary code cannot call it, and it is not an ordinary func value. | Enter it in the table: `idt[32] = x86.InterruptGate(timer, 0x08, 0)` |
| E2580 | NoPanicHandler | A freestanding or kernel build has no operating system to report a crash to, so the program itself must say what happens when it panics (print to a serial port or screen, then halt). | Mark one function with //pu:panic: `func onPanic(p *rt.Panic) { ... }` |
| E2581 | DupPanicHandler | A program has exactly one panic handler, and another function is already marked //pu:panic. Remove //pu:panic from all but one of them. | `pluto explain E2581` |
| E2582 | PanicHandlerDecl | The runtime calls the panic handler, the function marked //pu:panic, with a description of the panic, and never expects it to return. | Declare it: `func onPanic(p *rt.Panic) { ... }` |
| E2583 | PanicHandlerRet | A panic stops the program: it does not unwind, so there is nothing for the panic handler to return to. | End the handler by halting: `for {` |
| E2584 | ContextWaits | Interrupt handlers run on top of whatever code the CPU was executing, and the panic handler on top of whatever panicked. | To hand work to normal code, use a non-blocking send: `select { case work <- item: default: }` |
| E2585 | ContextSpawns | Interrupt handlers run on top of whatever code the CPU was executing, and the panic handler on top of whatever panicked. | To hand work to a task, wake one that waits for it, or send without waiting: `select { case work <- item: default: }` |
| E2586 | InitAllocates | In a freestanding build, which every kernel is, a package-level initializer or an init function can reach an allocation: new, make, a map literal, an operation that makes a string at run time, or a call that reaches one. | Declare the variable without an initializer, and set it in the entry function after alloc.SetDefault. |
| E2587 | InitSpawns | Package initialization runs sequentially before main. Starting another task there could let it read package variables before initialization finishes. | Start the task from main or a function main calls: `func main() {` |
| E2588 | NoGenMetadata | A checked freestanding or kernel build tags heap pointers, and the runtime keeps their generations in metadata it allocates outside the heap. | Export a metadata source, or build with --gencheck=false for a deliberate unchecked build: `var metadata [4 << 20]byte` |
| E2590 | GoCapturingLiteral | A function literal that uses variables of the function around it reaches them in that function's stack frame. | Pass the values as arguments: `for i := 0; i < n; i++ {` |
| E2591 | GoBuiltin | A task statement cannot start a built-in function such as println or close directly. Wrap it in a function and start that. | `pluto explain E2591` |
| E2592 | BadScheduler | A program binds its scheduler with one package-level variable marked //pu:scheduler, whose type, not an interface, implements rt.Scheduler: NewTask, FreeTask, Spawn, Park, Wake and Yield. | `pluto explain E2592` |
| E2593 | NoScheduler | This program starts tasks, uses channels or waits in pluto/sync, so it needs a scheduler, and none is bound. | Bind the kernel's scheduler: `var scheduler kernelScheduler` |
| E2594 | GoFrameClosure | A function literal that captures variables, and a method value such as c.handle, keep their closure record (the code to call, with the captured variables or a copy of the receiver) in the frame of the function that makes them. | Pass the values the function needs, and start a function that takes them: `task func(n int, out chan int) {` |
| E2595 | SchedulerTimers | Timers need two things from the scheduler: a clock, its Now method, which returns monotonic nanoseconds, and a way to be called back, its ArmTimer method, which asks for rt.RunTimers to be called once a deadline has passed. | Give the scheduler a clock, and run the timers from the timer interrupt |
| E2600 | UnknownDirective | A comment that starts with //pu: and no space is a directive: an instruction to the compiler. This one has a name the compiler does not know, so it would do nothing. | Use one of the directives, spelt exactly: `func timer(frame *x86.InterruptFrame) { ... }` |
| E2601 | RetiredDirective | This directive was removed, so the line is a compile error instead of something the compiler reads. Where the compiler now works the fact out, delete the line; the program means the same without it. | Delete the directive: `func halt() {` |
| E2602 | MisplacedDirective | A directive belongs in the doc comment of the declaration it applies to: the lines of comment directly above it, with no blank line between. | Put it directly above the declaration it applies to: `func slow() { ... }` |
| E2603 | DirectiveArgument | Some directives take an argument, such as the symbol name in //pu:extern, and the rest take none. This directive was given text it does not take, or lacks the argument it needs, so the compiler would not understand it. | Write the directive alone on its line: `func slow() { ... }` |
| E2604 | GoDirective | A line comment that starts with //go: and no space is a Go directive. Plutonium does not read //go: comments, so this one would sit in the file looking as if it had an effect. | Write the //pu: directive, or delete the line. |

## E3000 to E3999: ownership, lifetimes and races

Views of frames (E30xx), closures (E31xx), owner types (E32xx), moves and drops (E33xx), scoped tasks (E34xx), data races (E35xx).

| Code | Name | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| E3001 | ReturnFrameView | A function returns a view of its own frame: a pointer to one of its local variables, a slice of a local array, a function literal that uses local variables, or an interface holding a copy of a value in the frame. | Return the value itself, which copies it, or moves it if it is an owner. To keep it at a fixed address after the function returns, allocate it. |
| E3002 | StoreFrameView | A view of the frame, such as a pointer to a local variable, is stored in memory that lives longer than the frame: a package variable, memory reached through a pointer the function was given, or memory that may be on the heap. | Store the value instead of a pointer to it, or allocate the value so that it lives as long as the place that keeps it. |
| E3003 | PassFrameView | A view of the frame is passed to a function that keeps it after returning: the function stores it in a package variable, in memory that outlives the call, or passes it on to something that does. | Give the function something that owns its memory, such as a buffer or a value allocated for it. |
| E3004 | GoFrameView | A task statement starts a task that runs on its own, and may still be running after the function that started it returns. | Pass the value itself, which copies it, or moves it if it is an owner. |
| E3005 | SendFrameView | A value sent on a channel may be received after the function that sent it returns. A view of that function's frame sent this way could then point at reclaimed memory. | Send the value itself, which copies it, or moves it if it is an owner. |
| E3006 | LoopFrameView | A pointer to a variable declared in a loop, or a function literal that uses one, is kept after the iteration that made it: stored in a variable declared outside the loop body, for example. | Use the pointer or call the function literal within the iteration, store values instead, or pass the value to the function literal as a parameter. |
| E3007 | BadResultHolds | //pu:resultholds p says that a function keeps its parameter p only for as long as its result lives: the result, an owner, holds p and gives it back when it is dropped, as alloc.Use's Restore does. | `pluto explain E3007` |
| E3008 | ResultHoldsOutsideStd | //pu:resultholds is a promise the compiler cannot check: that a function's result gives a parameter back when it is dropped, as alloc.Use's Restore gives back the allocator it installed. | Remove the directive. If the compiler then rejects a call because the function keeps an argument, pass memory that lives long enough, such as an allocated value or a package variable. |
| E3009 | TempViewKept | A view of a temporary owner or counted box is kept: stored in a variable, in memory or in an interface, or returned. | Pass the view to calls in the same statement, or keep the owner in a variable, which lives until the end of its scope, and take the view through that variable. |
| E3010 | EscapeLimit | The escape analysis of a function reached its memory limit (256 MB) or its work limit (a billion steps) before it could finish: the function holds more distinct pointers than the analysis can follow. | Split the function into smaller functions, each handling part of the work: `func handle(req *Request) {` |
| E3100 | ClosureReturned | A function literal that uses variables of the function around it, and a method value such as c.handle, are closure records: the code to run, with where each captured variable is or a copy of the receiver. | Make the closure in the function that returns it, and return it by value: `func counter() func() int {` |
| E3101 | ClosureRegionLoop | A function that returns a closure builds it in a region its caller provides. | Use the closure within the iteration: `for _, n := range sizes {` |
| E3102 | ClosureRegionCycle | A function that returns a closure builds it in a region its caller provides, and that region holds the regions of the calls whose closures the function returns in turn. | Build the closures in a loop instead of by recursion, or keep their state in a value the caller owns, such as a struct with a method. |
| E3201 | DropNotOwner | A method named Drop runs automatically when a value is destroyed. | `pluto explain E3201` |
| E3202 | MustBeOwner | An owner owns memory or another resource and releases it when it is dropped, so it moves instead of being copied. | `pluto explain E3202` |
| E3203 | UnnamedOwnerStruct | A struct that contains an owner owns what that owner owns, so it must be an owner too, and only a named type can be declared an owner. | Declare a named owner type for the struct. |
| E3204 | BadOwnerKind | owner may mark a struct, an array, an integer, a pointer or unsafe.Pointer, or an interface type. | `pluto explain E3204` |
| E3205 | OwnerAlias | owner can only appear in a type definition, type T owner .... An alias (type A = T) is another name for an existing type and has that type's kind; it cannot add a mark of its own. | `pluto explain E3205` |
| E3206 | BadDropSignature | Drop runs automatically when an owner is destroyed. The compiler calls it with no arguments and ignores any result, so it must have no parameters and no results. | `pluto explain E3206` |
| E3207 | OwnerTypeArg | Generic code copies the values of a type parameter freely unless its constraint is marked owner. | `pluto explain E3207` |
| E3208 | BadTakeArg | take(p) moves the value p points to out of its place and leaves the zero value there. It needs the place's address, so that it can write the zero value back: a pointer such as &x.field, &s[i] or a pointer variable. | `pluto explain E3208` |
| E3209 | BadUnsafeDropArg | unsafe.Drop(p) destroys the value p points to, as the end of its owner's life would: it runs the value's Drop method and then drops its fields. | `pluto explain E3209` |
| E3210 | BoxOfInterface | owned[T], shared[T] and synced[T] hold one object of type T on the heap. | `pluto explain E3210` |
| E3211 | BadWeakElem | A weak reference refers to an object that counted references keep alive, without keeping it alive itself, so that structures with back pointers can be freed. | `pluto explain E3211` |
| E3212 | OwnerConversion | Converting a plain value into an owner type makes a new owner of whatever the value refers to: a file descriptor, a page frame. | `pluto explain E3212` |
| E3213 | MapOfOwner | A map copies its keys and elements as Go's map does: v := m[k] and range give copies of them. | Store a counted reference to the value instead: a synced[T] or shared[T] copies by counting, and the last copy releases the value. |
| E3214 | OwnerOperator | An operator other than a comparison is applied to a value of an owner type. | Convert the owner to its underlying type, which reads its value and moves nothing, and apply the operator to the result. |
| E3301 | UseAfterMove | A value of an owner type owns memory or another resource. Assigning it, passing it by value, returning it, sending it or storing it moves it instead of copying it, so that what it owns has exactly one owner. | `pluto explain E3301` |
| E3302 | UseMaybeMoved | A variable of an owner type is moved on some paths to this point and not on others, for example in one branch of an if, or in an earlier iteration of a loop. | Use it before the move, give it a new value on the path that moves it, or declare it inside the loop so that each iteration has its own. |
| E3303 | MoveOutOfPlace | An owner can be moved only out of a whole variable. A field, an element, a value reached through a pointer or a package variable would still believe it holds the owner, and the owner would be released twice. | Use take(&place) to move the value out and leave the zero value behind, a pointer (&place) to look at it without moving it, or Clone to copy it. |
| E3304 | RangeCopiesOwner | A range loop with a value variable copies each element into it. Copying an owner would leave two values that both release what it owns, so the elements of a slice or array of owners cannot be ranged over by value. | `pluto explain E3304` |
| E3305 | MoveCaptured | A function literal uses the variables of the function around it where they live. | Pass the owner to the literal as an argument instead, or move it before or after the literal runs. |
| E3306 | CopyOwners | copy, and append of a whole slice (append(s, t...)), duplicate the elements they copy. Duplicating owners would leave two values that both release what each owns. | Move the elements one at a time with take, or copy each one explicitly with Clone. |
| E3307 | DropThroughView | Drop releases what an owner holds, and runs by itself when the owner is dropped. | Call Drop on the owner itself, or leave the zero value behind with take. |
| E3308 | OwnerFromLender | Converting an owner to an ordinary interface such as any lends it: the interface looks at the owner, which still belongs to the variable that was converted. | `pluto explain E3308` |
| E3309 | IndexOwner | x[k] on a library container calls its Index method, which returns a copy of the element. When the elements are owners, the copy would be a second owner of what the element owns. | Use the container's methods instead: one that returns a pointer to the element to look at it (Ptr), or one that removes or replaces it to move it out. |
| E3310 | VariadicOwners | Variadic arguments are passed in an array that the function sees as a slice. A slice is a view and never owns its elements, so owners passed that way would be released by nobody. | Pass the owners one at a time, or in an owner of its own such as a vec.Vec. |
| E3311 | DeferInnerOwner | Deferred calls run when the function returns. An owner declared in an inner block is dropped when that block ends, before the deferred call would run, so the call would use what the owner had released. | Declare the owner at the top level of the function, or do the work at the end of the block instead of deferring it. |
| E3312 | SliceLitOwners | A slice literal keeps its elements in an array that the slice only looks at. Owners stored there would be released by nobody. | Use an array literal, which is an owner of its elements, or a vec.Vec. |
| E3313 | StaleView | A view taken from an owner held in a local variable (&c, a slice of a local array of owners, a method value c.M, c.Slice()) looks at memory that the variable owns. | Use the view before the owner is moved, or move the owner only after the last use of the view. If both are needed, move a copy made with Clone. |
| E3314 | LostView | A view of an owner held in a local variable may be used only while the variable keeps the value the view was taken from. | Keep the view in a local variable or a field of one, or move the owner only where no such view of it exists. |
| E3315 | ConsumingMethodValue | A method whose receiver is an owner type taken by value consumes its receiver: calling it moves the receiver into the method. | Call the method directly, or use the method expression T.M, which takes the receiver as its first argument when it is called. |
| E3401 | ScopeOutlivesVar | A task started by s.Task holds a pointer, slice or function literal that looks at a variable whose storage is reused before s waits for the task. | `pluto explain E3401` |
| E3402 | ScopeRace | A task started by s.Task uses a variable, or memory a variable points to, at the same time as another task or the function that started it, and one of them writes it. | `pluto explain E3402` |
| E3403 | ScopeNotPartitioned | Several tasks started by s.Task write elements of one slice or array, and the compiler cannot see that no two of them write the same element. | `pluto explain E3403` |
| E3404 | ScopeMoveInUse | A variable is moved or dropped while tasks started by s.Task may still use it. Moving an owner leaves the variable empty, and dropping it frees what it owns, so the tasks would use freed memory. | Wait for the tasks first, with s.Wait(), then move or drop the variable. |
| E3405 | ScopeMoved | A sync.Scope that has started tasks is moved: assigned, passed or returned. The tasks it started find it at its address, to tell it when they return, so after a move nothing would wait for them in the right place. | Keep the Scope in the variable that started the tasks. To wait for the tasks elsewhere, pass the work instead, or call s.Wait() before the Scope goes. |
| E3406 | ScopeConcurrentCall | A function literal is passed to a function that calls it from several tasks at once, and the literal writes a variable it captures. | Use an atomic type for the variable, or lock a mutex around the write in the literal. |
| E3407 | ScopeTakenWrite | A task started by s.Task changes a variable that it takes: the variable's block (a loop body, or the loop's own variables) may end before s waits for the task, so the task gets its own copy of the variable when s.Task runs, as... | Declare the variable inside the function literal if only the task needs it. |
| E3501 | RaceSendView | A pointer or slice is handed to another task, as an argument of a task statement or a value sent on a channel, but what it points to may change while both tasks can use it. | `pluto explain E3501` |
| E3502 | RaceNoLock | Data that several tasks use is written without a lock that guards it: a package variable written by code more than one task runs, or a field of a synced[T] object. | `pluto explain E3502` |
| E3503 | RaceUnguarded | Data that several tasks use is read without the lock that guards it. | Hold the lock (a sync.RWMutex's RLock is enough, or an rt.Lock for data a handler uses) around the read. |
| E3504 | RaceReleaseNotHeld | A lock is released where the code that releases it does not hold it. | `pluto explain E3504` |
| E3505 | RaceLockCopied | A value that holds a lock is copied out of a variable, field, element or dereference. | `pluto explain E3505` |

## E4000 to E4999: packages and modules

Finding, loading and naming packages; `pluto.mod`.

| Code | Name | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| E4001 | NotMainPackage | pluto build and pluto run build a program, and a program starts in package main, at func main. The directory given holds a different package, which can only be imported by a program or tested with pluto test. | `pluto explain E4001` |
| E4002 | NotPackageDir | pluto test takes a directory holding a package, or the import path of a standard library package such as pluto/strings. | `pluto explain E4002` |
| E4003 | TestDirName | A package outside any module is imported by its tests under the name of its directory. That name is reserved here, since main and pluto/... | Declare a module in the directory above: `module example.com/project` |
| E4004 | TestMainPackage | pluto test builds a program of its own that calls the tests, so it cannot test package main, which already is a program. | `pluto explain E4004` |
| E4005 | StdPackageMissing | Import paths that start with pluto/ name packages of the standard library, and this one does not exist. | `pluto explain E4005` |
| E4006 | PackageNotFound | The import path is inside this program's module, as declared by its pluto.mod file, but no directory exists at the matching place. | `pluto explain E4006` |
| E4007 | ImportNoModule | Without a pluto.mod file, a program is a single package that can import only the standard library (paths under pluto/). | Create pluto.mod in the top directory: `module example.com/project` |
| E4008 | ImportOutside | A program can import the standard library (paths under pluto/) and packages of its own module (paths under the module path in pluto.mod). | `pluto explain E4008` |
| E4009 | ImportCycle | Packages import each other in a circle. A package must be compiled after every package it imports, so a circle has no order that works. | `pluto explain E4009` |
| E4010 | NoSourceFiles | The package's directory has no .p files for this build. Either it has none at all, or every file is left out by a //pu:build line or a file name suffix such as _linux.p for the target and mode being built. | `pluto explain E4010` |
| E4011 | ExternalTestPkg | Test files in Plutonium belong to the package they test. A _test.p file in a package named x_test, which Go allows, is not supported. | `pluto explain E4011` |
| E4012 | MixedPackages | All the .p files in one directory must belong to the same package, so they must all start with the same package clause. | `pluto explain E4012` |
| E4013 | BadConstraint | A //pu:build line is a boolean expression over build tags, using && (and), \|\| (or), ! (not) and parentheses, such as //pu:build amd64 && !kernel. | `pluto explain E4013` |
| E4014 | BadModFile | The first line of a pluto.mod file must be the word module followed by the module path. | Write the first line as: `module example.com/project` |
| E4015 | ReservedModule | Import paths under pluto/ belong to the standard library, so a module cannot use one as its path. Choose another, such as a domain you control followed by the project name. | `pluto explain E4015` |
| E4016 | NoMainFunc | A program starts by calling func main in package main, and this package does not declare one. | Add a main function: `func main() {` |
| E4017 | ReadPackage | The compiler could not read the package's directory. Check that the path exists and that you have permission to read it. | `pluto explain E4017` |
| E4018 | BadTestSignature | pluto test runs the functions in _test.p files whose names start with Test or Benchmark. Such a function must take exactly one parameter, a *testing.T for a test or a *testing.B for a benchmark, and return nothing. | Declare it like this: `func TestParse(t *testing.T) {` |

## E5000 to E5999: assembling and linking

The assembler, linker and object files.

| Code | Name | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| E5001 | UndefinedSymbol | The linker joins the compiled program with its assembly, C and object files, and found a symbol that is used but defined nowhere. | `pluto explain E5001` |
| E5002 | RelocOverflow | The compiled code reaches every symbol with a 32-bit offset, so code and data must all lie within 2 GiB of each other. | `pluto explain E5002` |
| E5003 | MultipleDefs | Two objects define the same symbol. This happens when a .s, .c or .o file defines a function that Plutonium code also defines, when a //pu:export name is also defined in C, or when two C files define the same global. | `pluto explain E5003` |
| E5004 | AssemblerError | The GNU assembler rejected a .s file of the program. Its messages follow, with the file's own name and line. | `pluto explain E5004` |
| E5005 | CCompilerError | The C compiler rejected a .c file of the program. Its messages follow. C files are compiled freestanding: there is no C library, so headers such as stdio.h are not available. | `pluto explain E5005` |
| E5006 | LinkFailed | The linker failed. Its messages follow. If a linker script was given with --ldscript, check that it exists and places every section the program has. | `pluto explain E5006` |
| E5007 | PerCPUNotAtZero | Per-CPU variables are reached at their offset from the GS base, which only works if the linker places the .percpu section at address 0, with the Plutonium object first. | `pluto explain E5007` |
| E5008 | ToolNotFound | Plutonium uses the system's GNU assembler (as), linker (ld) and, for .c files, C compiler (cc, or $CC). | `pluto explain E5008` |

## E9000 to E9999: compiler errors

A bug in the compiler. Report it with the program.

| Code | Name | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| E9001 | InternalError | The compiler failed on a program that passed type checking. This is a bug in the compiler, not in your program. | `pluto explain E9001` |
| E9002 | ImplementationLimit | The program goes past a limit of this compiler. The parser accepts expressions, statements and types nested up to 100000 levels deep, and the type checker up to its own nesting limit, which is lower when its stack runs short. | Split the deep expression or type into named parts: `a := f(g(x))` |
